lessons.title: Choosing a bee site
lessons.html:
What makes a good apiary site?

An apiary (bee site) is a place where hives are kept. The site decides how much honey the colonies make, how healthy they stay and how safe people and animals are around them. In South Africa we work with two subspecies of the honeybee: the African bee (Apis mellifera scutellata) in most of the country and the Cape bee (Apis mellifera capensis) in the southern and western Cape. African bees are quick to defend their hive, so site planning is a safety matter, not only a production matter.

Forage

  • Bees need nectar (energy) and pollen (protein) for most of the year. Survey flowering plants within about two to three kilometres.
  • Useful sources include eucalyptus, aloes, acacias and other indigenous trees, fynbos, citrus and other orchards, sunflower, canola and lucerne.
  • Draw up a flowering calendar for the area. Gaps in flowering mean the colonies will need moving or feeding.
  • Do not overstock: too many hives on one site compete for limited forage.

Water

Colonies need clean water every day, especially in hot weather to cool the hive. A reliable natural source or a provided water point with floats so bees do not drown should be close by, but not so close that bees foul a household water supply.

Shelter and microclimate

  • Protect hives from strong prevailing winds with natural windbreaks.
  • Provide afternoon shade in hot areas; morning sun helps bees start foraging early.
  • Avoid frost pockets, flood-prone river banks and very damp low ground.

Access

You need to reach the site with a bakkie in all seasons for inspections, feeding and harvesting full supers, which are heavy. But the site should not be visible from public roads, to reduce theft and vandalism.

lessons.title: Safety, neighbours and legal requirements
lessons.html:
Keeping people and animals safe

Defensive African bees can sting people, dogs and livestock in large numbers. Serious injury or death is possible, especially in people who are allergic.

Distances and placement

  • Place hives well away from houses, schools, roads, footpaths, kraals, stables and places where animals are tied up. Tethered animals cannot escape attacks.
  • Keep hive entrances facing away from paths and work areas.
  • Use hedges or fences to force bee flight paths upwards, above head height.
  • Put up warning signs at the site entrance.
  • Check local by-laws for minimum distances in peri-urban areas.

Permission and registration

  • Get written permission from the landowner before placing hives. Agree on access times, rent (often paid in honey or ZAR), and who to contact in an emergency.
  • Beekeepers in South Africa must register with the national Department of Agriculture. Find out the current requirements and keep your registration up to date.
  • Movement of bees between the Cape bee region and the rest of the country is restricted to prevent Cape bees invading African bee colonies. Never move colonies across that boundary without checking the regulations.

Pesticides

Agree with farmers nearby that they will warn you before spraying insecticides. Many crop chemicals are toxic to bees. Labels registered under Act 36 of 1947 often contain bee warnings. If spraying is planned, close or move hives as advised.

Personal safety

  • Always wear a full bee suit, veil, gloves and boots. Use a lit smoker.
  • Work in pairs and carry a phone.
  • If stung, scrape the sting out quickly with a fingernail or blade and move away from the hive.
  • Signs of a severe allergic reaction include swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing, dizziness and collapse. This is an emergency: call for medical help immediately. Anyone with a known allergy must carry their prescribed medication. First-aid skills must be learnt from an accredited first-aid provider.

lessons.title: Setting up and maintaining the site
lessons.html:
Preparing the site

  1. Clear grass and bush in and around the hive area to reduce the risk of veld fire. Make a firebreak where needed.
  2. Level the ground for hive stands.
  3. Install hive stands. Raising hives off the ground keeps them dry, makes work easier on the back and protects against ants, toads and honey badgers.
  4. Protect against honey badgers, which can tip over and destroy hives. Use high stands, strap hive bodies together, or suspend hives from wires between posts.
  5. Set out hives a few metres apart, with entrances in slightly different directions and with landmarks, so returning bees do not drift into the wrong hive.
  6. Set up a water point if there is no natural water.
  7. Fence the apiary if livestock graze in the camp, so cattle do not rub against and topple hives.

Security

  • Brand or mark hives with your registration or name.
  • Keep a site register: GPS position, number of hives, owner contact details and landowner agreement.
  • Ask the landowner and farm staff to report disturbances.

Site maintenance

  • Visit regularly to check stands, straps, entrances and water.
  • Keep grass short around hives during the dry fire season.
  • Check colonies for strength, queen status, pests such as wax moth and small hive beetle, and diseases. Report suspected notifiable bee diseases such as American foulbrood to the authorities.
  • Record forage conditions so you can plan when to add supers, when to harvest and when to move colonies to a better site.

Evaluating the site

After a season, compare honey yield per hive, colony survival, swarming and absconding with other sites. Poor results may mean too many hives, poor forage, disturbance or pesticide exposure, and the site may need changing.

Key points

  • A good site has reliable forage, water, shelter and all-weather access.
  • Place hives well away from people, roads and tethered animals.
  • Get landowner permission, register as a beekeeper and follow bee movement rules.
  • Use stands and straps to protect against honey badgers, ants and damp.
  • Wear full protective clothing and treat severe allergic reactions as an emergency.
